title: Black holes big and small appear to follow the same rule when launching jets
freshness: Published September 17, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: When black holes feed on matter, they can blast some of it back into space as powerful jets. A new study finds that black holes ranging from stellar remnants to supermassive giants appear to switch on these jets at the same stages of their feeding cycle, despite their enormous difference in size.
whyItMatters: This suggests that one basic set of physics may govern how all feeding black holes behave, from relatively small ones made by dying stars to the giants at galaxy centres. A rule that works across such different scales turns seemingly erratic black-hole eruptions into something astronomers can begin to predict.

body:
## A feeding cycle that used to look chaotic

When a black hole pulls in gas, it does not swallow everything quietly. Some of that material is flung back out as a jet — a narrow, fast stream that can shine in radio waves and, over long timescales, help reshape the galaxy around it. Astronomers have long suspected that this messy eating follows the same basic physics whether the black hole is a stellar remnant only about ten times the mass of the Sun, or a supermassive giant millions of times heavier.

The obstacle has been watching those rules play out. Stellar-mass black holes in our galaxy can swing through a feeding cycle in days or weeks, so astronomers can catch the moment a jet switches on. A typical supermassive black hole in an active galaxy evolves over thousands of years. No observing campaign can sit with one of those systems long enough to see it cross the critical point.

## Using torn-apart stars as a stopwatch

A *Nature Astronomy* paper by Adelle Goodwin of Curtin University’s International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research and Andrew Mummery of the Institute for Advanced Study uses tidal disruption events as a workaround. In a tidal disruption event, a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and is shredded. Debris then forms a compact disk that can evolve in years rather than millennia — a human-length movie of a giant black hole feeding.

The team assembled optical, ultraviolet, X-ray, and radio observations of twenty such events, drawing on telescopes in America, Australia, India, South Africa, and space. In ten of those events they could model both the feeding rate and the timing of the radio outflow well enough to ask a precise question: at what stage of the meal does the jet turn on?

## Two switches, one familiar threshold

They found two distinct launching phases. The first is early, while the black hole is feeding at extreme, super-Eddington rates — more material than the theoretical limit where outward radiation pressure would balance gravity. The second comes much later, hundreds to thousands of days after the star is torn apart, when the feeding rate has fallen to about two percent of that Eddington limit.

That later mark is the result that travels. The same roughly two-percent threshold is already known to trigger a state change and a compact jet in stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way. In the new sample, delayed radio flares clustered around that scale, while prompt flares clustered at or above the Eddington rate. The authors argue that one scale-invariant process, not two unrelated recipes, governs jet launching across this huge range of black-hole masses.

That also helps explain a puzzle around these events: why some supermassive black holes blast out a jet right after shredding a star, while others stay quiet for months or years and then suddenly fire. Different events can simply be caught at different points of the same feeding cycle.

## Why a universal rule would matter

If the switch really is shared, jet launches stop looking like random eruptions and start looking like something astronomers can time. The paper offers a framework for predicting which black holes will launch jets and when, which could help observers point scarce telescopes — including the coming Square Kilometre Array — at the right moment instead of sampling blindly.

A population check in the study finds that this picture also lines up with how often radio outflows are seen. Only a minority of tidal-disruption disks are expected to go super-Eddington, matching current prompt-radio detection rates of roughly 30–50 percent. About 40 percent are expected to pass through the two-percent threshold in an observable window of a few years, close to independent estimates of how often delayed radio flares appear.

## What still needs care

This is a carefully modelled sample, not a census of every black hole. Only ten events had data good enough to pin down both the disk and the outflow timing. Strongly jetted, relativistic disruptions were set aside because their light is dominated by the jet rather than a measurable disk. The disk model is also less trustworthy in the super-Eddington regime, though the authors note that this uncertainty would tend to under-predict feeding rates there, which would not erase the high-rate prompt-outflow group. Launch dates assume a roughly constant outflow speed, with extra uncertainty for compact jets.

Treat the linked paper as the authority for the technical claims. The result is strong evidence that a shared accretion-rate threshold exists, not a guarantee that every quiet black hole will fire a jet on cue.

## What to explore next

The natural next question is to watch more tidal disruption events as they fade, and to see whether later radio outbursts keep arriving when the feeding rate crosses that same two-percent mark.
